Q3: I rarely used AI when I took courses regularly. Only once my coursework began focusing on professional development and career preparation have I begun experimenting with using AI to assist with feedback on early paper/proposal drafts and identifying appropriate funding opportunities for which to apply. Given the types of courses I have most recently taken, it also seemed to be a fair opportunity to gain some experience (and gauge my own interest) with using generative AI more extensively since I did not engage with it much in previous courses, aside from  using an advanced copyeditor for a bit (e.g., a grammar-checking tool).
Q4: Regarding my research, I have engaged with generative AI to generate feedback on proposal/chapter outlines regarding organization, stylistic flow, and copyediting. I have also engaged with AI using an approach similar to Google Scholar when literature searching, which has helped me identify a short list of citations to then fwd/back cite through Google Scholar/library databases as appropriate. I retain autonomy over idea generation, writing and composition, literature review and synthesis, theoretical reasoning, study design, and data analysis. A few times, I engaged with AI as a tool to challenge and identify inconsistencies with my interpretation of other scholars' arguments/findings. These reviews happened specifically after I received notes and revisions from human reviewers (revise and resubmit, advisor/committee notes, etc.). An area where I practice extremely selective non-use of AI regards uploading data due to caution around the risks associated with potential data breaches, dissemination of unpublished and/or sensitive information, and other privacy concerns. While I am confident in my ability to deidentify data as necessary, I tend to exercise an abundance of caution at this time. Regarding data interpretation, I often use more example prompts to create templates rather than prompts related to my study. If anything, particularly for quantitative research, I may engage back and forth with a generative AI chat to generate an explanation (with cited references) about the math behind any statistical tests rather than trusting the output, doing what I can to retain agency over analytical interpretations. I am comfortable with using AI to specifically debug challenging statistical code; however, I tend to attempt it myself first because I value my own skill, understanding, and professional and scholarly growth.

AI in 2026 is smarter than AI in last year and the years before, but it still doesn't do a good enough job in literature review. 
For graduate students, it is essential for them to 

1. be familiar enough with the literature to an extent that he/she will have a good idea on who is who, who said what, where a new research idea might potentially fill a gap, rather than letting AI tell them what to do and what not to do. To put it simply, they should be able to engage in meaningful academic conversations by themselves.

2. learn and understand the research methods and statistical analysis skills, to an extent that he/she would still be able to function as a qualified scholar when all the sophisticated AI technology is somehow not available. In other words, they should remain competent in doing research in the old school fashion.

3. always be aware of and show respect to the moral, legal, and ethical boundaries when using AI. For instance, not to upload interview transcripts or quantitative survey data to AI platform for analysis.

Q4: I use AI to help me refine my arguments, as a sounding board for ideas, and to help revise and edit writing. The line for me is basically I want my writing and ideas to be original to me, but I'm fine using AI to do things that people (myself or others) would take much more time to do (editing for grammar; collecting literature, etc.) so that I can concentrate my time and energy on the stuff that is original to me and my work.

Q3:
I usually decide based on the type of task and what I am supposed to learn from it. I use AI most often when I already have my own ideas but need help organizing them, checking my reasoning, improving my writing, or working through technical issues such as coding or statistical analysis. I also sometimes use it to help me understand a difficult reading or concept, but I try to go back to the original material rather than relying only on the AI summary.

I am less likely to use AI when the assignment is meant to test my own understanding directly, when the instructor does not allow it, or when using AI would basically replace the main intellectual work of the assignment. In general, I see it more as a tool for feedback, clarification, and problem-solving than something that should produce the work for me.
Q4: For my AP or dissertation, I will use AI as a research assistant rather than as a substitute for making research decisions. I use it to help brainstorm possible questions, organize literature, troubleshoot code, think through alternative model specifications, and clarify how to present results. I find it especially useful when I already have a specific question or problem and want to work through it more efficiently. At the same time, I am more cautious when it comes to theoretical arguments, measurement decisions, interpreting findings, and deciding what belongs in the final paper, because those are parts of the research where I think I need to make and defend the decisions myself. I also try to verify citations, statistical results, and factual claims independently rather than assuming that AI is correct.
Q6: I think AI can be very useful for graduate work, especially for non-native English speakers. Writing and polishing academic English can take a substantial amount of time even when the underlying ideas are already clear, so AI can reduce some of that language burden and allow students to focus more on the substantive and intellectual parts of their work. I also find it useful for iterative problem-solving, such as getting feedback on an argument, identifying alternative ways to approach a problem, or troubleshooting technical issues. At the same time, I think graduate students still need to be able to evaluate what AI produces rather than simply accept it. Clearer norms about appropriate AI use in research, writing, coding, and collaboration would also be helpful.
